summary: Defines procedures and protocol mechanisms to measure packet loss, one-way and two-way delay, and related metrics in MPLS networks. Providers need these measurements to monitor service level agreements and for planning and troubleshooting.

plainLanguage.summary: Network providers promise customers certain speeds and reliability. This describes ways to count lost packets and time them as they cross MPLS networks, so promises can be checked.

questions: what is mpls loss and delay measurement
how is packet loss measured in mpls
what is the difference between direct and inferred loss measurement
subtitle: How two MPLS routers count lost packets and time each other's replies, using small query and response messages.

tldr.problem: Provider service level agreements depend on measuring packet loss and one-way and two-way delay, and operators also need that visibility for planning and troubleshooting.
tldr.mechanism: A querier sends loss measurement (LM) and delay measurement (DM) messages over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel. The responder adds its own packet counters or timestamps and reflects the message back, so the querier can compute loss and delay from the four values.
tldr.outcome: The protocols are a Proposed Standard, designed to be simple enough for hardware processing. RFC 6374 has been updated by RFC 7214.

today: RFC 6374 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2011 and has been updated by RFC 7214. A minimal subset of the protocols for MPLS Transport Profile networks is described in RFC 6375.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Many service provider service level agreements (SLAs) depend on measuring packet loss and one-way and two-way delay, plus related metrics such as delay variation and channel throughput. RFC 6374 specifies two closely related protocols for this in MPLS networks: one for loss measurement (LM) and one for delay measurement (DM).

Both are intended to be simple and to support efficient hardware processing. They run over the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh, RFC 5586) and work for Label Switched Paths, pseudowires and MPLS sections (links). They can be used continuously (proactive) or on demand, and they use a simple query/response model in which one node, the querier, measures both directions.

The RFC notes that OWAMP (RFC 4656) and TWAMP (RFC 5357) already measure IP networks. Those protocols are not streamlined for hardware processing, rely on IP and TCP, and lack support for IEEE 1588 timestamps and direct-mode LM, which is why a separate MPLS design was written.
sections.plainLanguage: Network companies promise customers their data will arrive fast and mostly intact. This document gives them a simple way to check that promise by counting lost packets and timing trips.

sections.title: Query and Response Measurement
sections.content:
The basic scenario has two nodes, A and B, joined by a bidirectional channel. A sends a query to B, and B sends back a response. Four reference points, T1 to T4, mark when the query and the response are sent and received.

For loss, A puts the count of packets it has transmitted into the query (A_TxP). B appends the count of packets it has received (B_RxP) and, when it replies, the count it has transmitted (B_TxP). A adds the count it received (A_RxP). Because counters at the two ends may not start in step, loss is computed as a delta between two successive messages: transmit loss is the packets A sent minus the packets B received, and receive loss is the reverse. Arithmetic is modulo the counter size.

For delay, the query carries the transmit timestamp T1, B adds the receive time T2 and its own transmit time T3, and A adds T4. The two-way channel delay is (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2), and the round-trip delay is T4 - T1. One-way delays (T2 - T1 and T4 - T3) require synchronized clocks, while the two-way figures do not.

The RFC also describes throughput measurement (LM messages with timestamps), delay variation (derived from one-way delay), unidirectional measurement, loopback measurement and a dyadic mode. It does not specify a dyadic operational mode.

Counters must not wrap ambiguously between two messages, so the LM message rate MUST be high enough. The RFC gives an example: a 32-bit counter on a 100-Gbps link with a 64-byte minimum packet can wrap in about 22 seconds. This bound is called the MaxLMInterval.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask a friend to count how many balls you threw and how many they caught. Comparing the two numbers shows how many balls fell on the way. Writing the time on each ball shows how long they flew.

sections.title: Direct and Inferred Loss Measurement
sections.content:
The packets that are counted decide which loss measurement mode applies. In direct mode, the counted packets are the data-plane packets flowing over the channel. It can provide perfect loss accounting, but packets must not be sent or received between the moment a counter is read and the moment the LM message is sent or processed. This may require special support from hardware-based forwarding.

Direct LM can be hard or impossible to apply to an LSP when the label at the receiver does not exist or does not identify a unique sending node. The RFC names Penultimate Hop Popping and LDP-based LSPs as cases where this happens.

In inferred mode, the counted packets are special test messages generated by the sender, or other packets that serve as a good proxy, such as packets of a BFD session. It gives only an approximate view of loss but is typically applicable where direct LM is not.

Other practical points in the RFC include Equal Cost Multipath (only one path's delay is usually measured, and misordering degrades loss accuracy), measuring to an intermediate node by setting the TTL, and the need for implementations to state where their measurement points sit and which packets are in the loss measurement scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting every real car on a road is exact but needs special equipment. Counting only a few marked test cars is easier and gives a good guess.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
LM and DM messages travel in packets with an MPLS label stack that ends in the G-ACh Label (GAL), followed by an Associated Channel Header (ACH) that identifies the message type. The RFC defines five ACH channel types: Direct Loss Measurement, Inferred Loss Measurement, Delay Measurement, and the combined Direct and Inferred Loss and Delay Measurement types. All integer values are in network byte order.

The loss measurement message starts with Version (currently 0), Flags, a Control Code and a Message Length. It then carries data format flags, an origin timestamp format, a Session Identifier, a DS field for the traffic class being measured, a 64-bit Origin Timestamp and four 64-bit counter fields. The R flag marks a response and T marks a traffic-class-specific measurement. The X flag says 64-bit counters are in use, and B says the counters hold octet counts rather than packet counts.

The delay measurement message has the same first row, then the Querier, Responder and Responder's Preferred timestamp formats, a session identifier, the DS field and four 64-bit timestamps. A combined loss/delay message carries both the timestamps and the counters.

Counters and timestamps are laid out so that transmit values always sit at the same fixed offset and receive values at another, which the RFC says may matter for hardware processing. A query puts its transmit value in the first slot. The responder copies the first two values into the third and fourth slots and writes its own values into the first two.

An optional TLV block can follow. Type and Length are 8 bits each, so a Value can be up to 255 bytes. Types 0 to 127 are mandatory and 128 to 255 optional; an unrecognized mandatory TLV in a query must be answered with an Unsupported Mandatory TLV Object error. Defined TLVs are two kinds of padding, Return Address, Destination and Source Address, Session Query Interval and Loopback Request.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is like a form with boxes: who is asking, what kind of question, a tally of packets or a clock reading, and an optional extra notes page at the bottom.

sections.title: Timestamp Formats and Control Codes
sections.content:
Four timestamp format values are defined: 0 null, 1 sequence number, 2 the NTP version 4 64-bit format, and 3 the low-order 64 bits of the IEEE 1588-2008 Precision Time Protocol format. The default is format 3, the truncated PTP format, and implementations MUST support it. They SHOULD also be able to read NTPv4 timestamps, and support for others is optional.

Appendix A explains the choice. The document first proposed NTP as the default, but NTP has not gained traction as the protocol for high-quality timing infrastructure, while IEEE 1588 PTP has become the de facto time transfer protocol in networks engineered for accurate time distribution. Converting between the two formats in real time without loss of accuracy is not trivial.

The Control Code field says what a query asks for or what a response reports. A query can request an in-band response (0x0), an out-of-band response (0x1) or no response (0x2). A response is 0x1 for success, codes 0x2 to 0x5 for notifications that the data is not usable, and 0x10 to 0x1D for errors such as Unsupported Version, Authentication Failure or Administrative Block.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clocks can show the time in different styles, like a 12-hour and a 24-hour clock. The document picks one style everybody must know, so any two devices can still agree.

sections.title: Running a Measurement Session
sections.content:
A measurement operation is a session controlled by the querier: a sequence of queries on one channel with a common session identifier. A session can be as short as one DM query used to "ping" a remote node, or it can last for the life of the channel. The querier SHOULD run a SessionResponseTimeout timer, and an error response MUST end the session.

The Session Query Interval TLV lets both ends agree on a query rate. The querier sends it with a value of 0, the responder answers with its minimum supported interval in milliseconds, and the querier then picks an interval greater than or equal to that. Responders SHOULD rate-limit incoming queries.

For loss, the querier sets Counter 1 to its transmit count, and the responder sets Counter 2 to its receive count, copies the counters, and sets Counter 1 to its transmit count in the response. Direct LM excludes G-ACh packets by default. If messages are lost or misordered, the querier SHOULD treat the interval as unmeasurable and discard its stored state, using a MaxLMIntervalLoss threshold to spot impossible loss counts.

For delay, a responder sets its Responder Timestamp Format equal to the querier's format if it can write it, and otherwise to its own preferred format. If the formats in a response would differ, the Control Code MUST NOT be Success and is set to Data Format Invalid. An implementation that supports only one format simply discards responses whose formats do not match.
sections.plainLanguage: A measuring game has rules: how often to ask, what to do if a reply never comes, and when to stop and say something is wrong.

sections.title: Congestion, Manageability and Security
sections.content:
Proactive measurement adds load to the network and to the end nodes. Operators should pick transmit rates that do not stress resources unduly. A querier SHOULD track lost measurement messages against a Measurement Message Loss Threshold and suspend the operation if it is exceeded, so as not to worsen congestion, and tell the user.

The RFC also requires implementations to disclose their capabilities, such as which metrics, channel types, timestamp formats, loss modes and counter sizes they support.

On security, the protocols assume the path and the far end were already verified by existing MPLS mechanisms such as BFD. Where that is not available, receiving the G-ACh channel types SHOULD be disabled, and implementations MUST be able to disable them per channel type. The protocols remain open to injection and man-in-the-middle attacks, which would only compromise measurement quality, and the RFC says an attacker able to do this could already cause far greater damage. The RFC states that cryptographic mechanisms that sign or encrypt measurement packets without degrading measurement are not currently available. It suggests basic sanity checks at the querier and IPsec for out-of-band responses over IP.
sections.plainLanguage: Measuring too often can clog the road you are measuring, so go gently. Also, only trust a measurement if you already know who is on the other end.

data.title: Loss Measurement message after the ACH

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: R (query or response), T (traffic-class specific) and two zero bits.

fields.name: Control Code
fields.desc: Identifies the query or response type.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message in bytes, including any TLV block.

fields.name: DFlags
fields.desc: X for 64-bit counters, B for octet counts, and two zero bits.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Session Identifier
fields.desc: Set by the querier and copied in the response.

fields.name: Counter 3
fields.desc: Copy of the other end's Counter 1.

fields.name: Counter 4
fields.desc: Copy of the other end's Counter 2.

items.label: Sequence number
items.desc: A simple 64-bit sequence number for message ordering.

items.label: Truncated IEEE 1588 PTP
items.desc: 32-bit seconds followed by 32-bit nanoseconds. The default, which MUST be supported.
